title: Allergen Awareness
blurb: The 14 allergens, the golden rule of never guessing, and how to stop allergens reaching a free-from dish.
siteNotes: Where the accurate allergen information is kept for each menu (your manager will show you).
Who the chef or supervisor to tell is on each shift.
How allergen orders are flagged and prepared separately in the kitchen.
legalNotes: The 14 allergens that must be declared: Food Information Regulations 2014 (retained EU Regulation 1169/2011, Annex II). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2014/1855

Natasha's Law: pre-packed-for-direct-sale food must carry a full ingredient list with allergens emphasised, in force in England from 1 October 2021: Food Information (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2019.
CHECK: the trainer says allergen orders should be prepared separately. Current Food Standards Agency guidance supports this; confirm it matches the venue's allergen procedure.

cards.title: Allergen Awareness
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- name the 14 allergens that must be declared
- follow the golden rule of never guessing
- stop cross-contamination reaching an allergen dish

cards.title: A meal out can be life-threatening
cards.body:
For most people a meal out is a treat. For someone with a food allergy, the wrong dish can be life-threatening.

A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) can come on in minutes and can be fatal. That is why allergens are taken so seriously in law.

cards.title: The 14 allergens
cards.body: There are 14 allergens that must be declared by law. You do not have to memorise every dish, but you DO have to know where to find the accurate allergen information and use it every single time.

cards.title: Never guess
cards.body:
If a guest tells you about an allergy, take it seriously. Tell a chef or supervisor straight away and check the allergen information before you promise anything.

If you cannot be certain a dish is safe for that guest, do not serve it. An extra two minutes is better than a risk with someone's life.

items.title: Tell and check
items.text: Tell a chef or supervisor and check the allergen information.

items.title: Only then promise
items.text: Not certain? Do not serve it.

cards.title: Allergens travel
cards.body: An allergen can transfer onto an otherwise free-from dish through shared boards, utensils, fryers or hands. Allergen orders should be prepared separately and carefully.

cards.title: Natasha's Law
cards.body:
Natasha's Law means pre-packed-for-direct-sale food needs full ingredient labelling.

> When in doubt, always check. The guest is trusting us with their health.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Know the 14 allergens and where to find the allergen information
- Never guess: tell a chef or supervisor and check
- Not sure a dish is safe? Do not serve it
- Keep allergen orders separate from shared boards, utensils, fryers and hands
- Pre-packed-for-direct-sale food needs full ingredient labelling

cards.q: How many allergens must be declared by law?
cards.why: There are 14 allergens that must be declared by law.

cards.q: A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) can be fatal.
cards.why: Anaphylaxis can come on in minutes and can be fatal.

cards.q: What is the golden rule when it comes to allergens?
options: Never guess
Ask the guest to check
Trust the menu wording
Serve it if it looks plain
cards.why: Never guess. Check the allergen information every single time before you promise anything.

cards.q: Celery is one of the 14 named allergens.
cards.why: Celery is on the list of 14, alongside cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish and others.

cards.q: A guest tells you they have a nut allergy. What should you do?
options: Guess whether the dish is probably safe
Serve it and hope for the best this time
Tell a chef or supervisor and check the allergen info
Tell them nuts are rarely used here
cards.why: Take it seriously, tell a chef or supervisor straight away and check the allergen information before promising anything.

cards.q: If you can't be sure a dish is safe for an allergic guest, you should still serve it.
cards.why: If you cannot be certain a dish is safe for that guest, do not serve it.

cards.q: What is 'cross-contamination' in the context of allergens?
options: An allergen passing onto a free-from dish via shared kit or hands
A guest picking food from a friend's plate
An allergen being left off the printed menu
Food being kept in the fridge past its date
cards.why: Cross-contamination is an allergen transferring onto an otherwise free-from dish through shared boards, utensils, fryers or hands.

cards.q: Which of these is a named allergen?
options: Tomato
Chicken
Garlic
Sesame
cards.why: Sesame is one of the 14. Tomato and chicken are not on the list.

cards.q: 'Natasha's Law' relates to labelling of pre-packed-for-direct-sale food.
cards.why: Natasha's Law means pre-packed-for-direct-sale food needs full ingredient labelling.

cards.q: Which is one way an allergen could accidentally get onto a 'free-from' dish?
options: Serving it on a clean plate
Using a shared chopping board
Plating it at the pass
Covering it in the fridge
cards.why: Shared chopping boards, utensils, fryers or unwashed hands can all carry an allergen onto a free-from dish.
